Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Anthropic closed at $81.91 on Tuesday, Nov 24. That was 1.3% below its $83 IPO price. It was its first close below the offer, on its fourth trading day.

Falling below the offer is common for giant tech IPOs. Of the 10 giant US-listed tech IPOs in our set, 8 closed below their offer price at some point. Most got back to it quickly. For the 7 that did, the median wait was 3 days.

A seller who wants to keep a tax loss waits 31 days to buy back. The IRS calls it a wash sale if you - or a spouse or related account - buy the same or a substantially identical security within 30 calendar days before or after a loss sale. In 5 of the 8 cases, the stock was lower 31 days after its first close below the offer.

The median move over that stretch was a fall of 7.7%. So a seller who waited bought back cheaper more often than not. The margin is small, though, and it shifts with how the window is counted.

How Did Anthropic Get Below Its IPO Price?

Anthropic's first close, on Thursday, Nov 19, was $97.17. That was 17.1% above the offer. It then fell for three straight sessions. The drops were 8.5% on Friday, 1.4% on Monday and 6.5% on Tuesday.

The S&P 500 fell only 0.50% on Tuesday. We have no company statement that explains the selling. By Tuesday's close, Anthropic was 15.7% below its first close.

Anthropic fell from $97.17 to $81.91 in three sessions, a 15.7% loss for day-one buyers. Selling to claim that loss for taxes means staying out of the stock for 30 days. How Often Did Giant IPOs Break Their Offer Price?

Our set is the 10 giant US-listed tech and internet IPOs since 2012 whose offer price we could confirm. They are Facebook (now Meta Platforms), Alibaba, Snap, Lyft, Uber, Snowflake, Airbnb, Rivian, Reddit and CoreWeave. Airbnb and Reddit have never closed below their offer. The other 8 all did.

title: CoreWeave banks prepare $4.5 billion Meta-tied loan sale next week, Bloomberg says
detail:
CoreWeave banks prepare $4.5 billion Meta-tied loan sale next week, Bloomberg says
Luke Juricic
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 12:30 PM CST 3 min read
CRWV
META
8306.T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investing.com -- CoreWeave Inc's (NASDAQ:CRWV) underwriting banks are preparing to launch a $4.5 billion debt sale as early as next week, leveraging the cloud provider's artificial intelligence infrastructure contract with Meta Platforms Inc (NASDAQ:META) to secure investment-grade terms. According to Bloomberg, bankers at Morgan Stanley and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. are structuring the transaction, which will be backed by graphics processing units destined for a Meta-dedicated data center in Dalton, Georgia.

Proceeds from the offering will be held in an escrow account, allowing CoreWeave to draw down capital incrementally to fund hardware deployments while amortizing the debt over the life of the loan. Although CoreWeave carries a junk credit rating, the structural backing of Meta's counterparty credit is expected to earn the facility investment-grade ratings. Initial pricing discussions suggest the loan could yield between 7% and 7.5%, with early indications of interest already matching the $4.5 billion deal size.

The financing effort arrives amid intensifying market scrutiny over the capital intensity and long-term returns of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Broader sector sentiment has been further unsettled as billions of dollars in loans tied to Chinese technology firms were recently paused following new U.S. restrictions on chip access, threatening Asia's expanding AI debt market.

Against that backdrop, CoreWeave's existing corporate debt has faced acute selling pressure despite the company beating both its own guidance and Wall Street estimates for full-year revenue earlier this month. On Wednesday, the cost to insure CoreWeave's debt against default over a five-year horizon jumped by the widest margin on record, with credit default swaps implying a greater than 70% probability of default within that timeframe.

The stark divergence between the company's standalone credit risk and its asset-backed borrowing capacity is underscored by secondary market trading. Trace data cited by Bloomberg shows CoreWeave's 9% senior notes due 2031 fell to record lows on Wednesday to yield 18%, more than double the anticipated yield on the Meta-tied facility, even as the company's delayed draw term loans continued to trade near par.

title: Jim Cramer’s 5 Long-Term Stock Picks

Jim Cramer’s 5 Long-Term Stock Picks
Syeda Seirut Javed

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A caller asked CNBC Mad Money's Jim Cramer in November whether to buy a stock near $140 or wait. Cramer thought the difference between paying $130 and $150 would look small on a chart 10 or 15 years later. Warren Buffett made a similar point in his 1996 shareholder letter. He looked for businesses he could understand, at prices he could justify, with earnings he expected to be substantially higher years later. Cramer has applied that thinking to entire industries. When investors soured on one corner of the market, he looked past the next quarter and pointed to developments he thought Wall Street was giving too little credit.

That approach puts the emphasis on what can sustain earnings. An aircraft engine can generate service revenue for years after delivery. A retailer that gains market share during a housing slump can capture more of the spending when buyers return. Both can be good businesses, but the price an investor pays determines how much of that future growth is already reflected in the shares. It is worth noting that when a parent asked how to invest $50,000 for a 12-year-old, Cramer put half in an index fund. He was more selective about what he'd buy with the other half.

The U.S. market's record shows what a longer holding period has historically done for diversified investors. From 1950 through 2025, the S&P 500's worst calendar-year total return was about −37%. The worst rolling 10-year period returned −1% a year, and the worst rolling 20-year period returned +6% a year, based on calendar-year data. Picking individual stocks carries a different risk. Arizona State University finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder found that slightly more than 4% of U.S. stocks listed since 1926 accounted for all net shareholder wealth creation in his study.

Cramer talked about that trade-off during a June sell-off. He said diversification means accepting that some holdings will lag while money pours into the market's hottest sector. He pointed to one stock the rally had left behind and explained why he was willing to keep it.

So, what are Jim Cramer's long-term stock picks? We provided the expanded list of Jim Cramer's 10 Long-Term Stock Picks here. The top 5 stocks are provided below.

Jim Cramer's 5 Long-Term Stock Picks

Methodology

We reviewed publicly available Jim Cramer comments, including ones made on Mad Money, through November 24. We selected stocks he backed for long-term ownership and gave more weight to recommendations he reaffirmed after earnings or a significant business development. For each stock, we measured the price change from the next trading day's regular-session close through November 23 and compared it with the S&P 500 over the same dates. We listed the stocks in ascending order of the hedge fund sentiment of each stock, according to Insider Monkey's Q3 database of over 900 hedge funds.
